stories.title: APOD: 2026 October 19 – Treble Clef: Unusual X-ray Hot Radio Source
stories.summary: The Treble Clef, an unusual radio structure spanning over 2 million light-years, is hypothesized to be a cloud of charged particles expelled by a supermassive black hole. Recent X-ray observations suggest these particles were reinvigorated by a shock wave from colliding galaxy clusters, offering clues about galaxy cluster interactions and universal evolution.

stories.title: Whatcha lookin’ at? Social anxiety heightens brain sensitivity to others’ gaze
stories.summary: A University of Michigan study found young adults with higher social anxiety showed stronger brain responses to mismatched gaze and mental state words, indicating heightened neural sensitivity to social cues. This sensitivity did not improve explicit judgments of gaze meaning and may contribute to increased worry, with potential benefits or drawbacks depending on social context.
stories.finding: A University of Michigan study found young adults with higher social anxiety showed stronger brain responses to mismatched gaze and mental state words, indicating heightened neural sensitivity to social cues. This sensitivity did not improve explicit judgments of gaze meaning and may contribute to increased worry, with potential benefits or drawbacks depending on social context.
stories.significance: This research offers a new perspective on social anxiety, suggesting it may not solely be a source of distress but could also involve an enhanced sensitivity to social cues. This sensitivity might have both benefits, such as noticing important signals, and drawbacks, like increased worry, depending on the social context.
stories.caveat: While individuals with higher social anxiety showed greater neural sensitivity to gaze meaning, this advantage did not translate into improved accuracy or speed in later explicit judgments. The study did not establish whether this sensitivity helps people navigate real-world social situations.
stories.localConnection: University of Michigan research in Ann Arbor.

stories.title: They get knocked down—but they get up again
stories.summary: University of Michigan researchers found that low doses of the herbicide dicamba can cause oxalis weeds to produce more flowers, a phenomenon known as hormesis. While this did not consistently lead to increased seed production or genetic changes in the weed population, it altered pollinator visitation patterns and flower size.
stories.finding: University of Michigan researchers found that low doses of the herbicide dicamba can cause oxalis weeds to produce more flowers, a phenomenon known as hormesis. While this did not consistently lead to increased seed production or genetic changes in the weed population, it altered pollinator visitation patterns and flower size.
stories.significance: This finding suggests that unintended exposure to low doses of herbicides, such as from drift, might inadvertently enhance weed reproduction rather than suppress it. This could have implications for agricultural practices and home lawn care, potentially making weed control more challenging.
stories.caveat: While the study found that oxalis produced more flowers, it did not consistently translate to increased seed production in the second year of the experiment. Additionally, plants with more flowers due to dicamba exposure had lower pollinator visitation rates, and their flowers were smaller. The study also focused on a single weed species, and other species or populations might respond differently.
stories.localConnection: University of Michigan research in Ann Arbor.

inputFacts.title: They get knocked down—but they get up again
inputFacts.summary: Low doses of the herbicide dicamba can cause the common weed oxalis (wood sorrel) to produce more flowers, a phenomenon known as hormesis. This effect is a single-generation response and does not appear to be heritable or lead to evolution in the oxalis population.

inputFacts.title: NASA’s SPHEREx Telescope Sees Menagerie of Brown Dwarfs
inputFacts.summary: NASA's SPHEREx telescope has observed chemically rich atmospheres in 37 brown dwarfs, revealing the presence of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane across a wide temperature range. The observations indicate that current theoretical models struggle to match the data for cloudy transitions in brown dwarf atmospheres.

inputFacts.title: Mollusk microbiome? It’s all in the family
inputFacts.summary: The composition of a mollusk's microbiome is primarily determined by its species (family tree) rather than its living environment. This means that mollusks of the same species will have more similar microbiomes, even if they live in different locations, than mollusks of different species living in the same environment.

inputFacts.title: NSF lays the foundation for the next generation of technologies and support for American talent
inputFacts.summary: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) is launching several new programs and initiatives, including an Office of Metascience, two Grand Research Challenge (GRC) prize competitions (Quantum+X GRC and Synthetic Multicellularity Grand Challenge), the NSF X-Labs Consortium, and a funding opportunity for Super Intelligence-Native Instruments (SINI) within the NSF Programmable Cloud Laboratories Network (NSF PCLNet). Additionally, NSF is investing in the National Math Stars and NextGen Workforce programs.
